title: Modern human "Deep Skull" at Niah Cave, Borneo
summary: In 1958 excavators in the West Mouth of Niah Cave, Sarawak, on Borneo, recovered a modern human skull called the Deep Skull. Later dating places it at about 45,000 to 39,000 years ago, most likely around 37,000, making it the earliest securely dated modern human remains in island Southeast Asia.

uncertainty.note: Sources give a range rather than a point: about 45,000-39,000 years ago with c. 37 ka most likely (Frontiers 2016), and an earlier radiocarbon date of c. 39,600 BP. Year -38000 is a rounded midpoint of -45000 to -34000 (St Andrews: human activity c. 46,000-34,000 years ago); BP-to-calendar conversion is approximate. The skull was found in 1958.

as_recorded.value: c45-39 ka and mostly likely around 37 ka

where.modern_name: Niah Caves, Niah National Park, Sarawak, Malaysia
where.historical_name: Niah Cave (Gua Niah), West Mouth, Borneo; no polity existed at this date

importance.justification: Earliest securely dated modern human remains in island Southeast Asia, bearing on early dispersal across the region.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the age: sources give 45-39 ka with c. 37 ka most likely, and the older c. 40,000 BP radiocarbon date was controversial. The pin is the UNESCO property centre, not the West Mouth trench.
